Quickstart¶

This guide introduces the basic py4radiation workflow for generating radiative heating, cooling and ion fractionn tables from custom spectral energy distributions (SEDs).

The examples use a continuous star-formation model from Starburst99, but the same workflow can be applied to other supported SEDs.

1. Preparing a radiation field¶

The SED class prepares the input SED into Cloudy-readable format.

For example, consider a stellar population with:

  • Continuous star formation.

  • Star-formation rate of 5 solar masses per year.

  • Stellar population age of 3 Myr.

  • Distance of 1 kpc from the source.

The corresponding SED can be generated using:

from py4radiation import SED

sed = SED(
    run_name="example",
    table_id="8b",
    sfr_msun_yr=5.0,
    distance_kpc=1.0,
    age_myr=3,
)

sed_path = sed.write_outfile()

print(sed_path)

The generated Cloudy input file is:

example_z0.0000e+00.out

The file contains the interpolated spectral shape and the absolute normalisation at 1 Ryd.

Starburst99 normalisation¶

Starburst99 Figures 7-12 contain stellar-only spectra, without the nebular continuum included in Figures 1-6.

The luminosity of continuous star-formation models (Figures 8, 10 and 12) scales with the star-formation rate.

For instantaneous-burst models (Figures 7, 9 and 11), the luminosity scales with the initial stellar mass.

The spectral flux density is calculated as

\[F_\nu = \frac{L_\nu}{4\pi d^2},\]

where \(L_\nu\) is the spectral luminosity and \(d\) is the distance from the source.

2. Generate Cloudy parameter files¶

The ParameterFiles class generates the parameter files required by pyCIAO.

The following example creates a small density-temperature grid for demonstration purposes:

from py4radiation import ParameterFiles

par = ParameterFiles(
    cloudy_path="/path/to/cloudy.exe",
    run_name="example",
    elements="H C N O",
    n_limits=(-9, 4),
    n_spacing=0.125,
    T_limits=(1, 9),
    T_points=321,
)

hc_parfile = par.hc_parfile()
ib_parfile = par.ib_parfile()

print(hc_parfile)
print(ib_parfile)

The generated parameter files are:

example_hc.par
example_ib.par

The first file configures heating and cooling calculations, while the second configures ionisation-fraction calculations.

Both reference the radiation-field file generated in the previous step.

Note

Replace /path/to/cloudy.exe with the actual path to your Cloudy executable.

Generate the SED and parameter files from the same working directory so that the generated radiation-field path is correctly referenced.

3. Execute Cloudy with pyCIAO¶

pyCIAO provides a command-line interface for executing Cloudy calculations.

Heating and cooling calculations can be started with:

pyciao example_hc.par --nproc 4

Ionisation-fraction calculations can be started with:

pyciao example_ib.par --nproc 4

The --nproc argument specifies the number of Python multiprocessing workers.

Each worker executes a subset of the Cloudy calculations defined by the parameter file.

The generated outputs are stored in the corresponding subdirectories:

hc/
ib/

Each directory contains a master .run file and the numerical maps generated by Cloudy.

The master .run file records the parameter combinations associated with the numbered calculations.

MPI execution¶

If py4radiation was installed with MPI support and a compatible MPI environment is available, calculations can also be distributed across MPI ranks.

For example:

mpiexec -n 4 pyciao example_hc.par

When multiple MPI ranks are detected, pyCIAO uses MPI instead of Python multiprocessing.

Note

The examples in this section execute external Cloudy calculations. You need a working Cloudy installation and valid parameter files.

4. Process heating and cooling tables¶

The HeatingCoolingTables class combines the individual heating/cooling maps into a single table.

from py4radiation import HeatingCoolingTables

hc = HeatingCoolingTables(
    run_dir="hc",
    run_name="example",
)

table_path = hc.write_table()

print(table_path)

This generates:

example_cooltable.dat

The default table contains:

  • Hydrogen number density in cm^-3.

  • Temperature in K.

  • Heating coefficient.

  • Cooling coefficient.

  • Mean molecular weight in atomic mass units.

By default, the heating and cooling rates are normalised by the square of the hydrogen number density.

The resulting coefficients have units of erg cm^3 s^-1 for this normalisation.

5. Process ionisation-fraction tables¶

The IonTables class combines the individual ion fraction maps into an HDF5 file.

from py4radiation import IonTables

ib = IonTables(
    run_dir="ib",
    run_name="example",
    elements="H C O",
)

ib.write_table()

This generates:

ib/example_iontable.h5

The HDF5 file contains logarithmic ionisation fractions for the selected chemical elements.

The dataset dimensions are ordered as:

(ionisation stage, density, redshift, temperature)

For calculations performed only at z=0, the data are duplicated at z=1e-4 to provide the redshift dimension required for Trident interpolation. This is not intended to show cosmological evolution, but a way to match with the expected table dimensions.

This additional redshift slice does not represent a separate Cloudy calculation.

6. Alternative radiation fields¶

The same workflow can be applied to other radiation sources supported by py4radiation.

Haardt & Madau (2012) background¶

To generate the metagalactic ultraviolet background at z=0:

from py4radiation import SED

sed = SED(
    run_name="hm12_example",
    table_id="HM12",
)

sed.write_outfile()

The original HM2012 tables provide the specific intensity \(J_\nu\).

py4radiation converts this quantity into

\[F_{\nu,\mathrm{equiv}} = 4\pi J_\nu,\]

in erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1.

Unlike stellar radiation fields, HM2012 does not require distance, star-formation-rate or stellar-mass scaling.

A local HM2012 table can also be supplied through the hm12_path argument.

Custom spectral energy distributions¶

Users can provide their own spectral luminosity tables.

The input must contain two columns:

  • Wavelength in Angstroms.

  • \(\log_{10}(L_\lambda)\), with \(L_\lambda\) in erg s^-1 Angstrom^-1.

For example:

sed = SED(
    run_name="custom_example",
    table="custom_sed.dat",
    distance_kpc=1.0,
)

sed.write_outfile()

The custom luminosity spectrum is converted to spectral flux density using the specified distance.
